The British Nationality (Regularisation of Past Practice) Act 2023 received Royal Assent on 29th June 2023. This act confirms the British citizenship of children born in Great Britain and Northern Ireland between 1 January 1983 and 1 October 2000, to a parent who was exercising a free movement right in the UK.
Youth Mobility Scheme amended to allow New Zealand nationals to extend their stay by 1 additional year.

The nationality good character requirement's criminality thresholds were aligned with those in Part 9 the Immigration Rules. Sentence-based threshold for a refusal of citizenship were reduced from four years to 12 months, and consideration of ‘spent periods’ for those with a sentence of between 12 months and four years was removed.

From 13 July 2023, the Streamlined Asylum Process was extended to apply to children’s non-legacy (‘flow’) asylum claims made from 28 June 2022 to 6 March 2023 for nationals of the same five high-grant countries.
On 17 July, changes were made to the student route to remove early switching to another visa route before completion of studies. There is an exemption to PhD students who can switch after 24 months.
Illegal Migration Act

Two transitional routes- family members of qualifying British citizens (FMQBC) and Zambrano primary carers- closed to new applications.  
The EUSS has remained open to FMQBC and Zambrano applicants with pre-settled status (or a pending EUSS application, administrative review or appeal) or with pending access to the EUSS via a relevant EUSS family permit.
A new validity requirement was introduced preventing illegal entrants from making a valid application to the EUSS as a joining family member.

On 9 August 2023 meeting the deadline for applying or having reasonable grounds for the delay became a requirement for a late EUSS application to be valid and for a Certificate of Application to be issued, confirming temporary protection of rights while the application is determined.
The Faciliated Returns Scheme (FRS) was expanded again to include all FNOs served a stage 1 deportation notice eligible. Previously only those with a custodial sentence met acceptance criteria.
In September 2023 automatic extensions of pre-settled status by 2 years started being applied to those approaching the expiry of that status who have yet to obtain settled status.
Youth Mobility Scheme amended to allow Canadian and Australian nationals to extend their stay by 1 additional year.

Following the enactment of certain sections of the Illegal Migration Act, the following policy changes went live on this date: 1) We updated criteria for caseworkers assessing credibility of asylum claims by explicitly setting out that factors such as the destruction of, or failure to produce an identity document, as well as refusal to disclose information required to access an electronic device like a phone passcode when asked, should be considered when assessing claims.  2) Clarification that the Home Secretary, rather than the Courts, will determine what constitutes a reasonable time period to detain a person for immigration purposes. This includes when they are being removed from the UK. When detainees challenge the length of their detention as unreasonable, the courts must take the Home Secretary’s view into account.

In March 2023, the Government announced that it intended to enable former members of Hong Kong military units discharged before 1 July 1997, to settle in the UK. This was done by extending the provisions of the settlement concession that already existed for former Gurkhas and their families, to Hong Kong military unit veterans and their families, and bringing both cohorts under the Immigration Rules.

Amendments to validity for student dependants and Graduate main applicants and dependants to clarify the requirement to obtain consent from a Government or international scholarship agency where the previous permission relied on their scholarship or sponsorship.

The Supreme Court concluded that deficiencies in the Government of Rwanda's arrangements for determining asylum claims could lead to risks of refoulement (returning refugees or asylum seekers to a country where they are liable to be subjected to persecution).

S.46 NABA was implemented. S.46 NABA amends s.10 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 to incorporate new provisions on notice periods and the scenarios where a notice period is not required. S.10 provides that a person who requires permission to enter or stay but does not have it may be removed. S.10 gives all individuals subject to enforced removal a statutory entitlement to a minimum notice period of 5 working days. It also creates a statutory requirement to inform the individual of the date of their removal, destination and route.

UK and Rwanda signed a new asylum partnership treaty, which will not come into force until ratified by both parties. This treaty partly replicates the terms of the original Memorandum of Understanding (April 2022) but with some significant changes.  It aims to deter dangerous and illegal journeys to the UK by relocating asylum seekers, and people arriving in the UK without permission, to Rwanda where they can apply for asylum.  The treaty is due to last until 13 April 2027 unless renewed.

The Government are launching a dedicated out of country settlement route for victims of transnational marriage abandonment. This will ensure that someone who is abandoned overseas is able to benefit from the settlement provisions in the new Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse. This consolidates provisions that were previously in Appendix FM and Appendix Armed Forces into Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse.

Swaziland’s name was changed to Eswatini on the list of Commonwealth countries in Schedule 3 of the British Nationality Act 1981. Togo and Gabon were added to the list of  Commonwealth countries in Schedule 3 of the British Nationality Act 1981 having joined the Commonwealth. This does not, however, give nationals of Togo and Gabon the right of abode in the UK, as they were not Commonwealth citizens when the 1981 Act came into force.
For courses starting on or after 1 January 2024, only research-based postgraduate students are now allowed to bring dependants (partners and children) to the UK.

The Immigration (Age Assessments) Regulations 2024 came into force on 10 January 2024. This instrument specifies the scientific methods (MRI and X-rays of various body parts) that may be used for the purposes of age assessments under section 50 or 51 of the Nationality and Borders Act 2022. These measures have not yet been operationalised.

came into force. Under these provisions, the Early Removal Scheme (ERS) has been extended from 12 months to 18 months before the earliest release date. This applies as long as at least 50% of the custodial sentence has been served – the sentence must be a minimum of five years and eleven and a half months. This should increase the number of FNOs that become eligible for the scheme and therefore increase the number of those returned to free up more prison spaces and ease the burden on the British taxpayer.

The Youth Mobility Scheme was amended to include nationals of Andorra and Uruguay. The age range has increased from 18-30 to 18-35 for Australian, Canadian and South Korean nationals. Australian and Canadian nationals are also now able to extend their stay by 1 additional year. The annual quotas for South Korea and Japan have been increased to 5,000 and 6,000 places respectively.
Introduction of Appendix Bereaved Partner which replaces the bereaved partner provisions within Appendix FM and Armed Forces rules.

Permitted Paid Engagements (PPE) has now been incorporated into the Standard Visitor route. Visa nationals must apply for a visit visa (PPE) in advance of travel to the UK and non-visa nationals must seek admission/entry at the UK border from an immigration officer. Any PPE must be pre-arranged prior to travelling to the UK and the PPE activity must be undertaken in 30 days of arrival as a visitor.
Those with permission to stay as a stateless person can sponsor a partner to come to the UK under Appendix FM – the family immigration rules.

Appendix Bereaved Partner was introduced into the Immigration Rules, replacing the provisions in Part 8, Appendix FM, and Appendix Armed Forces. The provisions for a dependent child of a Bereaved Partner are included in Appendix Bereaved Partner and the general grounds for refusal in Part 9 of the rules are applied to this route.

Introduction of new Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse replaced existing provisions for Victims of Domestic Abuse and their dependent children in Part 8, Appendix FM and Appendix Armed Forces of the Immigration Rules.  This provided a single set of Victim of Domestic Abuse rules for those applying for settlement.
Revised definition of a partner came into effect.

An update made to the Immigration Rules for Hong Kong BN(O) route whereby the requirement for partners to prove they had been living together in a relationship similar to marriage or civil partnership for at least the two years before the date of application was removed.

The Youth Mobility Scheme was amended to include nationals of India under the India Young Professionals Scheme. The route allows those aged 18-30 to live, work and study in the UK for up to 2 years, and has an annual quota of 3,000.

Introduction of the Migrant Victims of Domestic Abuse Concession to replace the Destitute Domestic Violence Concession. Eligible victims get a short period of LOTR (three months) with recourse to public funds on a discretionary basis. This enables them to access welfare benefits, fund safe accommodation, and make arrangements to leave the UK, or apply to stay in a capacity other than as a partner. Eligibility mirrors the new Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse with the addition of partners of those on work or study routes.

The Ukraine Permission Extension (UPE) scheme, announced on 18 February 2024, allows Ukrainian nationals and eligible family members in the UK to extend their stay for up to 18 months. Successful applicants can continue to live, work, study, and access public funds. Eligibility requires existing permission under a Ukraine Scheme, have been living in the UK since that permission was granted, and, for non-Ukrainian partners, an ongoing relationship with a Ukrainian national. UK-born children of Ukrainian parents with permission may also apply.

Amendments were made to the Immigration Rules: Appendix Ukraine Schemes to close the Ukraine Family Scheme to new applicants, amend the period of permission for new applications to 18 month (reduced from 36 months) for Homes for Ukraine and Ukraine extension scheme applications, and to reintroduce previously disapplied paragraphs of the General Grounds for Refusal. In addition changes were also made to policy guidance to require sponsors of applicants under the Homes for Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme to have settled status or be a British or Irish Citizen. These changes impacted the visa routes available to Ukrainians seeking temporary sanctuary in the UK as a result of the ongoing conflict in Ukraine.

Overseas care workers and senior care workers stopped from bringing dependants, and a new requirement for social care providers sponsoring these workers in England to be providing services regulated by the Care Quality Commission (CQC).

MIR - The minimum income requirement for those on partner visas was increased to £29,000 from 11 April 2024. This was the first increase for over a decade and the first step in tethering the MIR to the Skilled Worker Threshold as part of a wider package to reduce Net Migration.

Continuous residence - The standard requirements of Appendix Continuous Residence are being applied to Appendix Long Residence and Appendix HM Armed Forces (only in relation to settlement as a Partner or Child).  Applying Appendix Continuous Residence to Appendix Long Residence aligns the approach to permitted absences, including time periods and reasons for absences, with other routes.

Appendix Long Residence - The standard requirements within Appendix Continuous Residence, Appendix English Language and Appendix KOL UK (Knowledge of life in the UK) have been applied to the Long Residence route. Includes a policy change whereby applicants must have had their current permission for one year (or have been exempt from immigration control within the 12 months immediately before their application) to qualify for settlement on this route. This aligns the requirements of this route with wider requirements for settlement. Also includes changes to standardise the conditions for grants of temporary permission to stay on the Long Residence route.

The Armed Forces Rules - The changes separated the Armed Forces provisions into Appendix HM Armed Forces and Appendix International Forces and Civilian Employees to make it more transparent to whom the provisions apply. The minimum income requirement (MIR) to be met for HM Armed Forces personnel to sponsor a partner or dependent child(ren) was increased to £23,496 to tether it to the HM Armed Forces salary threshold for personnel on completion of training.

English language - Appendix English Language has been updated to reflect that International GCSEs are accepted as evidence of English language ability and to extend the Appendix to the following routes: Appendix Settlement Family Life, Appendix HM Armed Forces, Appendix Long Residence and Appendix Temporary Work – International Agreement.

Appendix Adoption - replaces existing provisions for children entering the UK for adoption in Part 8 of the Immigration Rules and comes into force on 6 June 2024. This will provide clearer and more consistent rules for adoption.
Replacement of Appendix Armed Forces with Appendix HM Armed Forces and Appendix International Forces – this is part of on-going work to ensure they are consistent with simplification work.
Enabled applicants to extend their permission to stay on the Hong Kong BN(O) route with access to public funds where they continue to meet the criteria
Enabled applicants on the BN(O) route to access an affordability fee waiver where they applied for an extension of 30 months permission
Allowed decision makers to add up to 28 days of existing permission onto a BN(O) applicant’s further permission to stay where the applicant applied for a 30-month visa
Allowed eligible family members of an individual who holds both BN(O) status and British citizenship to apply to the BN(O) route
Allowed Adult Dependent Relatives to apply later to join the main applicant in the UK, on the BN(O) route

Removed the requirement for partners and Adult Dependent Relatives to have their permission end on the same date as the main applicant where they can apply to join them later in the UK, on the BN(O) route

The Afghan Response Route is launched. The ARR was created in response to the February 2022 ARAP Data Incident and provided for certain individuals to be considered for eligibility for relocation to the UK.
Enabled those who were placed on immigration bail solely because they claimed asylum in the UK to apply to the BN(O) route

Expanding the immediate settlement provisions under Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse and access to the Migrant Victims of Domestic Abuse Concession to include a spouse, civil partner or durable partner with pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme (meaning that the relationship was formed before the end of the transition period on 31 December 2020), and their dependent children

Skilled Worker general salary threshold raised from £26,200 to £38,700, with updated lower thresholds maintained for Health and Care Workers and occupations subject to national pay scales.  “Going rate” salary requirements for individual occupations increased from the 25th percentile to the median full-time earnings for UK workers in those occupations.  Shortage Occupation List replaced by the Immigration Salary List, and removal of the “going rate” discount for occupations on the list.
Amendment to eligibility for student dependants clarifying the course requirements for a student to sponsor dependants when relying on government scholarships and sponsorships.
An agreement between the UK and Vietnam was signed to increase cooperation on dealing with illegal migration.

The Immigration (Guidance on Detention of Vulnerable Persons) Regulations 2024 enter into force. These amend the Statutory Adults at Risk in Immigration Detention Guidance to update the purpose and principles of the policy and place the ability to seek second opinions on professional evidence on a statutory footing.

The High Court in Belfast ruled that the provisions of the Illegal Migration Act 2023 are incompatible with article 2(1) of the Windsor Framework and should be disapplied in Northern Ireland.  It also declared other provisions to be incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights.
The Ukraine Extension Scheme closed to most new applications other than for children who are born in the UK to parent(s) who have permission to be in the UK under one of the Ukraine Schemes.

The British Nationality (Irish Citizens) Act 2024 received Royal Assent on 24 May 2024. It inserts new section 4AA into the BNA 81 which creates a new route for Irish citizens to register as a British citizen. Irish citizens making use of this route must have acquired 5 years' residence in the UK, and have not been absent past legislative threseholds. They must not have been in breach of immigration laws, and the section  is subject to sections 31, 32 and 36 of the Illegal Migration Act 2023 (restriction of eligibility for citizenship etc). The Act will come into force on a date that is set out in future regulations made by the Home Secretary, as allowed for by Clause 2(3) of the Act.
The Home Secretary launched the new Border Security Command, to boost Britain’s border security and deal with organised immigration crime.

The Home Secretary laid a statutory instrument to remove the retrospective application of the Illegal Migration Act. This allowed decision-makers to begin deciding asylum claims from individuals who arrived from 7 March 2023 onward.

The launch of Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS) Pathway 1 Separated Families route, which aims to reunite families unintentionally separated during the evacuation of Kabul. A 3-month referral window allows eligible individuals to make referrals to reunite family members and be resettled to the UK.
The Home Secretary announced new measures to boost Britain’s border security, including increased resource to target, dismantle and disrupt organised immigration crime networks.
Standard Determinate Sentence 40% (SDS40) came into force

The EU Settlement Scheme pending prosecution policy was amended, so that a pending prosecution does not prevent caseworkers progressing an application. If the applicant satisfies the eligibility criteria and suitability criteria (setting aside the allegations which are the subject of the pending prosecution), leave may be granted. If the applicant does not satisfy the eligibility criteria and suitability criteria (setting aside the allegations which are the subject of the pending prosecution), leave will be refused. If the applicant is subsequently convicted and given a custodial sentence, the case will be referred to FNO RC through the usual prison referral mechanism. Should FNO RC pursue deportation, a deportation order will invalidate any EUSS leave held under section 5(1) of the Immigration Act 1971.

The Home Secretary agreed to the G7 Anti-Smuggling Action Plan, aimed at fostering closer cooperation with G7 partners to bolster border security, combat transnational organised crime, and protect vulnerable individuals from exploitation by migrant smugglers.

The ECAA (Settlement) guidance was updated to incorporate the revised Appendix Continuous Residence elements as appropriate. This was needed as one of the conditions for settlement under the ECAA was completion of a continuous 5 year period of residence. The changes will come into force on 8/10/24.

A new validity requirement was introduced requiring a joining family member to apply to the EUSS within three months of their first (not latest) arrival in the UK since the end of the transition period (or later where there are reasonable grounds for their delay).
Introducing a fee waiver for bereaved partners who are destitute.
Former Home Secretary Yvette Cooper signed ato tackle people smuggling and organised crime networks operating across the region and in Europe.

Changes to the Immigration Rules (HC 334) were laid in Parliament setting out requirements for the Ukraine Permission Extension Scheme to launch on 4 February 2025 and to end the use of permission to travel letters from 13 February 2025
The Home Office temporarily paused decisions on Syrian asylum claims.
Specifying that time spent on the Ukraine Schemes does not count towards the qualifying period requirement for long residence.

The guidance was updated for Hong Kong BN(O) routes to clarify that individuals will no longer receive a Biometric Residence Permit and that dependent partners and Adult Dependent Relatives are not required to apply for the same length of permission as the main applicant

The maintenance requirement for students (to demonstrate they have the funds to support themselves while in the UK) increased from £1334 to £1483 per month up to 9 months for students studying in London, and £1023 to £1136 outside London
The Home Office introduced a new process to automatically convert eligible pre-settled status holders to settled status, without the need for them to make a further EU Settlement Scheme application.
The launch of the Ukraine Permission Extension (UPE) Scheme for applications from Ukraine visa scheme permission holders in the UK to extend their permission for up to 18 months.

The nationality good character requirement was amended so that anyone who enters the UK illegally or who arrives without a required valid entry clearance or electronic valid authorisation having made a dangerous journey, including small boat arrivals, will normally be refused British citizenship regardless of the time that has passed since their arrival. This change applies to citizenship applications made from 10 February 2025.

Changes to the Immigration Rules (HC 733) were laid in Parliament regarding requirements for the Homes for Ukraine Scheme and Ukraine Permission Extension Scheme and to close the variation of permission process for applicants who deferred their biometrics on the Homes for Ukraine Scheme.
The Afghan Resettlement Programme (ARP) was launched in March 2025, and brought together Government’s Afghan resettlement schemes into a single, efficient pipeline (ARAP; ACRS & ARR).

The BN(O) guidance was updated to reflect the change in application fees in accordance with The Immigration, Nationality and Passport (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations 2025.

An amendment has been introduced to the validity EU Settlement Scheme validity requirements, enabling a non-EEA national applicant to use a UK-issued biometric residence card or permit which has expired by up to 18 months as proof of their identity and nationality and, where they use such a biometric residence card, not require them to re-enrol their fingerprint biometrics.

EU Settlement Scheme guidance was updated to reflect the Court of Appeal judgment in R (Ali) v Secretary of State for the Home 
Department [2024] EWCA Civ 1546, which found that, where they were resident in the UK before the end of the transition period, the right to reside of a child aged over 21 or a dependent parent is not lost where they ceased to be dependent as a result of exercising their right to work in the UK.

Changes to the EU Settlement Scheme suitability requirements, allowing for an application to be refused on 
suitability grounds, without a deportation or exclusion order being in place, where the applicant’s conduct before the end of the transition period meets the relevant EU law public policy test applicable under the Citizens’ Rights Agreements.

Amending the Immigration Rules, specifically the ETA validity requirements (Appendix ETA) to clarify that eligible (non-visa) nationals must obtain an ETA before travelling to the UK from Ireland - 24 June 2025.
Syrian asylum caseworking resumed following a pause in December 2024.

Changes to the EU Settlement Scheme continuous residence requirements, enabling a pre-settled status holder to maintain their status and be eligible for settled status where they have been resident in the UK for at least 30 months in total in the most recent 60-month period, as opposed to the previous requirement to generally have been absent from the UK for no more than six months in any 12-month period.

Changes to guidance for the EU Settlement Scheme to reflect that, where the applicant is an EU, other EEA or Swiss citizen, or their family member (including a joining family member or a family member who has retained the right of residence by virtue of a relationship with them), who has extant pre-settled status and has then obtained another form of immigration leave, such as settlement under Appendix Victim of Domestic Abuse, they will retain their pre-settled status alongside the other form of immigration leave. There is no deadline for them to apply, if they wish, for settled status under Appendix EU once they are eligible for it based on their continuous residence in the UK.
ARAP and ACRS closed to new applications or referrals.
ARR discontinuation announced by SSD

The Graduate Dependant relationship requirement was amended to add a clause that would enable caseworkers to refuse dependant graduate applications when the main applicant’s visa application had been refused
The Student Dependant relationship requirement was amended to ensure the wording of the dependant relationship requirement for the Graduate and Student routes remain aligned

Changes to Skilled Worker visas following the Immigration White Paper – raising the skills threshold to RQF6 (graduate occupations), introducing an interim Temporary Shortage List, raising salary thresholds, and closing adult social care applications from overseas.

Awas signed with Iraq, strengthening its strategic partnership as agreed in the November 2024 joint statement. This included a Returns Declaration of Intent, which established more streamlined formal processes to return those with no legal right to be in the UK swiftly.

This treaty enables the return of small boat arrivals from the UK to France, with an equal number of individuals eligible to come to the UK through a new legal route. This is a pilot scheme which has the potential to undermine the business model of criminal gangs.

Announced widening of the 'Deport Now, Appeal Later' scheme, having previously covered 8. This provides that appeals can be heard by video link from certain countries where the technology is available.
The application process for Ukrainians who travelled to the UK with a Permission to travel letter to vary their permission closed to new applications.
Refugee Family Reunion route paused for new applications made after 15:00 on this date. All those applying as the partner /child of a person with protection status now to apply under Appendix FM.

Amendment to the Modern Slavery Statutory Guidance so that individuals who: have received a negative Reasonable Grounds or Conclusive Grounds decision in the National Referral Mechanism, and who the Secretary of State for the Home Department intends to remove to a country that is a signatory to the Council of Europe Convention on Action Against Trafficking in Human Beings and European Convention on Human Rights, are not able to request a reconsideration of that decision.

The window in which FNOs can be removed under the Early removal scheme (ERS) has been changed via a statutory instrument. The ERS used to allow the ability to be removed up to 18 months before their custodial release date subject to having served 50% of their custodial sentence but MoJ expanded this window to allow removal up to four years before the custodial release date subject to having served (a reduced) 30% of their custodial sentence.

The Deprivation of Citizenship Orders (Effect during Appeal) Act 2025on 27 October 2025. The Act prevents those who have been deprived of British citizenship from regaining that status – and so preventing those who are overseas from returning to the UK – until all onward appeals have been determined, or the time period in which to appeal has elapsed.

Thedesigned to reduce illegal migration and accelerate the return of illegal migrants. New measures include: the use of biometric data sharing in the identification process, accelerating the issuance of documents, and a commitment to intensified cooperation to dismantle immigration crime networks and enhanced deterrence messaging.

Eligibility for the High Potential Individual route expanded to incorporate graduates from universities ranked in the Top 100 of the relevant global universities rankings and an annual cap of 8,000 applications

Alignment of the grounds for cancelling pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme on or before the holder’s arrival in the UK into line with those for curtailing it in-country, so that, where proportionate, this can be based on the fact that the person never met, as well as where they have ceased to meet, the requirements of Appendix EU.

Theon the Government’s asylum and returns policy introduces:1. deterrence‑focused measures designed to reduce irregular arrivals;2. system‑wide changes to increase decision‑making and removals; and3. the expansion of safe and legal routes, alongside new temporary protection rules.Alongside this, there will be specific capped routes for skilled workers and students, giving those with the right qualifications a chance to build a future in the UK.

‘Part 9: grounds for refusal’ has been replaced with ‘Part Suitability’ and all references to ‘Paragraph 39E’ have been removed and substituted with ‘Exceptions for Overstayers’ in accordance with the change to the Immigration Rules introduced in November.
Campsfield IRC opened on 01 December 2025.

The Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 received Royal Assent on 2 December 2025. Following royal assent in December 2025, the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act introduced measures on 5 January and 2 February 2026, including new offences and strengthened enforcement powers to disrupt organised immigration crime, through enhanced search and seizure powers, improved data-sharing, and tighter controls on immigration leave and bail. A further measure commenced on 5 March 2026 enabling searches where a deportation order is under consideration, with remaining provisions being implemented on a phased basis through 2026 towards full implementation by year end.
32% increase to the Immigration Skills Charge for the Skilled Worker and Global Business Mobility routes
As of 23 December 2025 the Modern Slavery Statutory Guidance was updated to the effect that public order disqualification decision making is paused.

Alignment of the grounds for cancelling pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme on or before the holder’s arrival in the UK with those for curtailing it in-country, so that, where proportionate and subject to a right of appeal, this can be done where it is more likely than not, that, after the end of the transition period, they have assisted another person fraudulently to obtain, or to attempt to obtain, entry clearance to, or leave to enter or remain in, the UK.

Amendment to the EU Settlement Scheme (EUSS) travel permit route to enable all EUSS status holders to obtain an EUSS travel permit where they are unable to update their UK Visas and Immigration account, for example with the details of a new travel document, from outside the UK.
Closure of the Service Providers from Switzerland route.

On 26 January 2026, the Statement of Evidence Form (SEF) ‘opt out’ pilot was introduced for Unaccompanied Asylum Seeking Children (UASC) and Accompanied Asylum Seeking Children (AASC) claiming in their own right aged 16 and 17. The pilot allows eligible children to proceed to a substantive asylum interview without completing a Statement of Evidence Form (SEF), provided they have secured legal representation and consented to the pilot.

In response to the threat of visa penalties, due to poor cooperation on returns, the governments ofto improvements to returns processes, enabling the swift and efficient return of those nationals with no right to be in the UK.

The government has introduced new regulations that make working illegally a breach of conditions of asylum support, providing a mechanism for the suspension or discontinuation of asylum support when this condition is breached. Two Statutory Instruments (SIs) were laid on 5 March 2026 to make these changes. The first SI ‘The Asylum Support (Amendment) Regulations 2026’ came into force on 27 March 2026 and applies to asylum seekers in receipt of Section 95 and Section 98 support. The second SI ‘The Immigration and Asylum (Provision of Accommodation to Failed Asylum-Seekers) (Amendment) Regulations 2026’ came into force on 2 June 2026, and applies to failed asylum seekers in receipt of Section 4 support. Policy guidance was published on 2 June to support implementation of the powers granted by the SIs.

Section 45 of the Sentencing Act 2026 has the effect of extending the duty to deport foreign criminals (as well as extending the definition under legislation of foreign criminals) from persons sentenced to 12 months or more imprisonment to also include persons given a suspended sentence of 12 months or more. This provision came into effect on 22 March 2026. 
Section 45 also extends the requirement of the Secretary of State, under the UK Borders Act 2007, to make a deportation order in respect of a non-British, non-Irish citizen convicted in the UK of an offence for which they were sentenced to a period of imprisonment of at least 12 months, unless an exception applies (for example, where deportation would breach the person’s European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) rights, or the UK’s obligations under the Refugee Convention); so that it also applies to those given a suspended sentence of at least 12 months.
In addition, subsection (2) of section 45 amends section 117D(4) of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 so that a person who has been given a suspended sentence of at least 12 months is a “foreign criminal” for the purpose of the Article 8 public interest considerations in section 117C, and all references to periods of imprisonment of a certain length of time in Part 5A include suspended sentences.

Changes to paragraphs 339QA and 339QB of the Immigration Rules, and the introduction of paragraphs 339QAA and 339QBA of the Immigration Rules. These changes reduce the duration of permission to stay on a protection route to 30-months for adults and accompanied children (including further submissions). Applies to claims lodged on or after 2 March 2026, commenced 26 March 2026.

A visa brake has been implemented for certain routes and nationalities from 26 March 2026. Under this brake, student visa applications made by nationals of Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan are now being refused, in addition to Skilled Worker visa applications made by nationals of Afghanistan. The visa brake is not intended to be permanent and the Government will keep it under review.

Changes to the BN(O) route include - Eligibility for the BN(O) route was expanded to BN(O)s’ adult children who were born on or after 1 July 1979; the term ‘Household Member’ has been replaced with ‘Adult Child’; references to the 90-day entry clearance vignette have been removed as applicants attending a visa application centre no longer receive a vignette; applicants can now verify their identity using the UK Immigration: ID Check app when applying for settlement and the guidance confirms the forms required to submit an application; and guidance has been updated to reflect the change in application fees in accordance with The Immigration, Nationality and Passports (Fees) (Amendment) Regulations 2026.
The application window for UPE increased from 28-days to 90-days before an applicant’s current Ukraine Scheme permission expires.

The UK and France signed anto strengthen operations to combat illegal migration in northern France and prevent crossings to the UK with a significant increase in dedicated human, technological and intelligence resources. For the first time, UK funding will include a flexible part to support actions to strengthen the effectiveness of the agreement. These actions will be subject to regular joint evaluation in order to analyse their impact on reducing the flow of illegal migration.

An amendment has been introduced to the EU Settlement Scheme validity requirements enabling non-EEA national applicant to use a UK-issued biometric residence card which has expired by up to 60 months as proof of their identity and nationality.

The Modern Slavery statutory guidance was updated in May 2026 to clarify how decision makers should consider when and how information about exploitation is disclosed as part of an overall assessment of credibility. In particular, decision makers are now guided to consider when information was shared and the opportunities an individual had to disclose it, and the reasons for any delay in disclosure, including trauma, fear of authorities, or safety concerns.
The first individuals eligible for the 24-month UPE extension were eligible to submit an application to extend their stay.

The Basic Compliance Assessment framework for Student sponsors was updated on 1 June, which introduced tighter compliance metrics for sponsors to pass and a new Red-Amber-Green rating system for sponsors. This is designed to improve sponsor recruitment practices.

The Government has revoked Regulation 5 of the Asylum Seekers (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2005, replacing the duty to provide asylum support with a discretionary power under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999. The revocation took effect on 2 June 2026; however, current arrangements for the provision of asylum support remain unchanged pending the development of a new policy framework.
